description_ru: Биография Фриды Кало: полиомиелит, трагическая авария, бурный брак с Диего Риверой и искусство, превратившее боль в автопортреты.
text:
Frida Kahlo liked to say that she had been born in 1910, the year the Mexican Revolution erupted, so that her life and her country might begin together. The truth was more prosaic. Magdalena Carmen Frida Kahlo y Calderón was born on the sixth of July 1907, in the blue-walled house in Coyoacán, then a village on the edge of Mexico City, where she would also die. Yet the little fiction reveals the essential Frida: a woman who edited reality with the same boldness she later brought to canvas, and who regarded biography as a medium, like oil paint, to be shaped to her purposes.

Her father, Guillermo, was a German immigrant who had reinvented himself as a photographer of buildings, and an epileptic of exacting temperament. Her mother, Matilde, was devout, practical and sometimes forbidding. Frida inherited her father's eye and her mother's iron. At six she contracted poliomyelitis, which left her right leg thinner than her left, and she was teased in the street as "peg-leg Frida." She answered the cruelty by wearing long skirts and thick socks, and by becoming the most mischievous girl in her class. She also took up boxing, cycling and, with a gang of fellow pranksters, the art of defying her teachers.

In 1922 she entered the National Preparatory School, one of the few girls among some two thousand students, intending to become a doctor. On the seventeenth of September 1925, when she was eighteen, she boarded a wooden bus with her sweetheart. The vehicle collided with a streetcar. An iron handrail pierced her pelvis, entering through her hip, and her spine, collarbone, ribs and right leg were broken in several places, while her foot was crushed. A passenger carrying a packet of gold powder was jostled, and the powder showered over her bleeding body, so that, it is said, onlookers cried out that the dancer had been transformed into a ballerina of gold.

She survived, though she would later insist that the accident had never really ended. She spent months in a plaster corset in hospital, and then at home, where boredom became unbearable. To distract her, her mother commissioned a special easel that could be attached to the bed, and installed a mirror in the canopy above it. Frida, confined to her back, found herself staring at the only model available. It was thus that she began the long series of self-portraits that would define her. "I paint myself," she explained, "because I am so often alone, and because I am the subject I know best."

By 1928 she had joined the Communist Party and, at a party, been introduced to Diego Rivera, the colossal muralist who was then the most famous artist in Mexico. She was twenty-one; he was forty-one, vast, married twice before, and notoriously unfaithful. When she asked him to assess her paintings, he declared that she was manifestly talented and should carry on. They married in 1929, a union that her parents described as that of an elephant and a dove. Frida adored the comparison, and later amplified it by painting herself standing next to her enormous husband, small, solemn and unblinking.

Their marriage was a prolonged and operatic collision. Diego pursued other women with undisguised appetite, eventually including her younger sister Cristina, an affront that Frida could scarcely forgive. She retaliated with lovers of her own, men and women alike, among them the sculptor Isamu Noguchi and, briefly, the exiled Leon Trotsky, who stayed at her family home in 1937. In 1939 the couple divorced, only to remarry the following year, and Frida wrote that she had suffered two accidents in her life: the bus, and Diego. The second, she added, was by far the worse.

Between 1930 and 1934 they lived in the United States, where Diego painted murals in San Francisco, Detroit and New York. In Detroit, in 1932, Frida suffered a miscarriage and, in response, painted Henry Ford Hospital, a raw, startling image of herself on a bleeding bed, tethered by red ribbons to emblems of her grief. She had always been unable to carry a pregnancy to term, and the sorrow is woven into her work as insistently as the flowers she braided into her hair. American critics, patronising and bemused, called her paintings fantastical. She disagreed, politely.

The French poet André Breton, meeting her in 1938, pronounced her a Surrealist. Frida rejected the label with some impatience. "I never painted dreams," she said. "I painted my own reality." Nonetheless, Paris welcomed her warmly, and the Louvre purchased her self-portrait The Frame, making her the first twentieth-century Mexican artist to be represented in its collection. She, meanwhile, thought the Parisian intelligentsia insufferable, and wrote to a friend that she would rather sit on the floor of a market in Mexico than endure another of those pretentious loafers.

Her style drew on Mexican folk art, on retablos, small devotional paintings on tin, and on the pre-Columbian figures that crowded her house. She dressed in the embroidered blouses and flowing skirts of the women of Tehuantepec, a costume that concealed her leg and the corsets she wore, and that also amounted to a declaration of identity. In total she produced roughly two hundred paintings, about a third of them self-portraits, which she described as her attempt to endure, rather than escape, her suffering.

The final decade was cruel. She endured some thirty operations, grew dependent on painkillers and alcohol, and in 1953 had her right leg amputated below the knee, after gangrene set in. That same year, when her first solo exhibition in Mexico opened, she was too ill to attend, so she arrived by ambulance and was installed, in a four-poster bed, in the middle of the gallery, where she held court amid the guests, singing and joking. She died on the thirteenth of July 1954, aged forty-seven. Her last painting, a still life of watermelons, bore two words in the flesh of the fruit: Viva la Vida.

Posterity has been generous. The blue house in Coyoacán is now a museum, visited by queues of pilgrims, and her face, with its unbroken eyebrows and defiant gaze, has become one of the most reproduced images in modern art, a verdict she would have greeted with a sardonic smile and a cigarette.

questions.question: In which year did Frida claim to have been born, and why?
questions.answer: 1910, the year of the Mexican Revolution.

questions.question: What happened to her on the bus in 1925?
questions.answer: It collided with a streetcar and an iron handrail pierced her pelvis.

questions.question: How did her parents describe her marriage to Diego Rivera?
questions.answer: As the union of an elephant and a dove.
